newsitem.title: USA: Shuttle astronauts start second spacewalk.
newsitem.headline: Shuttle astronauts start second spacewalk.

text.p: Astronauts from the shuttle Discovery carefully slotted a new targeting device into the Hubble Space Telescope early on Saturday to improve its aim at distant celestial objects.
Greg Harbaugh and Joe Tanner carefully removed an ageing guidance sensor and replaced it with a new device fitted with special optics to correct for Hubble's misshapen mirror.
"Ever so gently," cautioned Harbaugh as Tanner gingerly manoeuvred the 492-lb (223-kg) sensor, about the size of a baby grand piano.
"I think it's in there, yes sir!" Harbaugh said as the delicate instrument slid into place like a draw in a filing cabinet.
Tanner worked perched on the end of the shuttle's 50-foot (15-metre) robot arm, while Harbaugh assisted, tethered to the four-story telescope like a mountain climber.
At one point, Tanner had to steady Harbaugh while he made some tricky electrical connections by clinging onto his spacesuit backpack.
The new guidance sensor will give the telescope unprecedented pointing accuracy, comparable to focusing a laser beam on a small coin from 200 miles (320 km) away.

The $8 million device would be used to determine the position of stars about 10 times more precisely than ground-based telescopes. Astronomers also hoped to use it to detect tiny wobbles in the motion of nearby stars that might indicate the presence of an orbiting planet.
The astronauts then tackled the replacement of a broken tape recorder and a quick wiring job for the new guidance sensor.
The spacewalk was taking longer than expected, partly because mission control ordered additional inspections of Hubble's tattered and tarnished exterior.

The astronauts reported that the harsh environment of space had taken its toll on Hubble. They found paint had discoloured and in places foil insulation was torn and peeling away from the telescope's skin.

"The specific concern is if that starts breaking off then it could contaminate the optics and then degrade the capabilities of the telescope," said astronaut Jerry Ross, who watched the spacewalks from mission control.
Mission managers formed a team of engineers to consider ways of repairing the foil, which protects the telescope from harsh temperature changes as it orbits the planet.
The astronauts also spotted numerous space debris hits on the telescope's 40-ft (12-metre)-long electricity-generating solar panels.
"That's like somebody shot a small calibre bullet right through it," Tanner said as he videotaped one hole in the solar cells.
The two men began the spacewalk at about 10:30 p.m. EST on Friday (0330 GMT Saturday) as the shuttle orbited 360 miles (575 km) above the Pacific Ocean.

The final task of the astronauts' day would be to gently ease Hubble into a higher orbit with firings of the shuttle's precision manuevering jets. NASA wants to boost the telescope's altitude by about five miles (eight km) to prolong its lifetime.

Flight controllers at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Centre reported the two new scientific instruments installed on Friday during the first spacewalk of the mission appeared to be working properly. It would be about 10 weeks, however, before astronomers expected to get the first images and data.
Additional spacewalks were planned for Saturday and Sunday nights to complete the $350 million refurbishment of the orbiting observatory.

It was the first time astronauts have worked on the telescope since a 1993 mission repaired its blurred vision. Since that flight the telescope has provided definitive proof that star-devouring black holes exist and has reached puzzling conclusions about the age of the universe.
